text: The prior course's SOAR chapter established this generically: a playbook only works safely when every branch of its decision tree was already known in advance. Sentinel playbook design applies that same principle with one more dimension added — impact, not just whether a scenario is well understood.

The real question for any action inside a playbook isn't whether it can be automated — almost anything can be scripted. It's whether that action is low-risk and well-understood enough that being wrong, occasionally, costs very little. Confidence in the correct response matters, and so does how expensive it is if automation gets that response wrong.

Some categories pass that test clearly. Notifications — posting to Teams, sending an email, paging on-call — cost a few seconds of someone's attention if wrong. Enrichment, like checking a URL against threat intel, only adds information without changing anything. Tagging an incident is reversible and purely organizational. These are exactly the actions the worked example used two lessons ago, and that's not a coincidence.

Other categories fail that test even when the scenario is common. Disabling a user account is correct for a confirmed compromise, devastating for a legitimate user caught by a false positive. Isolating a production server is correct against confirmed malware, an outage-causing mistake if the detection was wrong. Blocking a sender domain is correct against malicious infrastructure, disruptive if it's actually a shared mail gateway.

That's why playbook design for actions like these typically inserts an approval step — the playbook still runs the enrichment and notification automatically, then pauses and waits for a human to approve the final, consequential action before taking it. A phishing playbook can fully automate the threat-intel check and the SOC notification, then pause for a human to approve quarantining the email organization-wide.

Automate the cheap, reversible, high-confidence parts; let a human approve the expensive, hard-to-reverse one. That's the whole of Sentinel automation design, and it closes this chapter. Next: Chapter 8's capstone, starting with writing a custom analytics rule in KQL from scratch.
